title: Market Structure
description: Concentration, entry barriers, contestable markets, HHI

concepts.title: Beyond the Textbook Cases
concepts.contentHtml:
Microeconomics teaches four canonical structures: perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, monopoly. Real industries fit none of them precisely.

Industrial Organization (IO) is the field that studies how real markets actually work — the strategic behavior of firms, the structure of industries, and the policy implications.

The classical IO triad: structure (concentration, entry barriers) → conduct (pricing, advertising, innovation) → performance (profits, prices, efficiency). The arrows go both ways — performance affects structure too.

Modern IO has moved beyond this static framework toward dynamic, game-theoretic, and empirical analyses. But the questions remain: how concentrated is this market? Why? What does it imply for prices, innovation, and welfare?

concepts.title: Measuring Concentration
concepts.contentHtml:
Two main measures of market concentration.

Concentration ratio (CRn): share of total market held by the top n firms. CR4 of 70% means the top 4 firms have 70% of the market.

Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI): sum of squared market shares (in percentages). HHI ranges from ~0 (perfect competition) to 10,000 (pure monopoly).

HHI weights large firms more, capturing both the number of firms and the inequality of their sizes. A market with one firm at 80% and twenty firms at 1% each looks more concentrated than one with five firms at 20% each, even if CR4 is similar.

US antitrust guidelines:

– HHI < 1500: unconcentrated

– 1500-2500: moderately concentrated

– > 2500: highly concentrated

Mergers raising HHI by more than 200 in concentrated markets get particular scrutiny.

concepts.title: Entry Barriers
concepts.contentHtml:
Whether market power persists depends on entry barriers — what stops new firms from coming in to compete?

Structural barriers: economies of scale (a new entrant must build at full scale or face cost disadvantage), capital requirements, network effects, learning curves, control of essential inputs.

Strategic barriers: incumbent behavior that deters entry — predatory pricing, capacity over-investment, exclusive contracts with suppliers.

Legal barriers: patents, licenses, regulations, tariffs, geographic restrictions.

Sunk costs: if entering requires irrecoverable investment, entry is risky and incumbent threats credible.

The Bain framework (1956): markets with high entry barriers can sustain high prices and profits indefinitely. Without barriers, even monopolies face contestable threats and behave more competitively.

concepts.title: Contestable Markets
concepts.contentHtml:
Baumol-Panzar-Willig (1982) contestable markets theory: even highly concentrated markets can perform competitively if entry and exit are costless.

The argument: a single incumbent in a contestable market can't charge monopoly prices, because doing so would invite hit-and-run entry. Knowing this, the incumbent prices at competitive levels even though it's the only firm.

The condition: perfect contestability — entry costs nothing, exit costs nothing, and entry is faster than incumbent response.

Real markets rarely meet these conditions, but the framework matters for policy. It implies the right question isn't just 'is this market concentrated?' but 'are entry barriers high enough to sustain market power?'

Some markets with few firms are quite contestable — taxi markets in cities with easy licensing, online retail with low entry costs. Others with many firms aren't — networks where switching is costly even if alternatives technically exist.

concepts.title: Modern Concentration Trends
concepts.contentHtml:
US (and to some extent global) markets have become more concentrated over the past 30 years.

Major trends:

– Tech/digital platforms: Google, Meta, Amazon dominate search, social, e-commerce.

– Retail: Walmart, Costco, Amazon dominate physical and online retail.

– Healthcare: hospital consolidation, insurer mergers, pharmacy benefit manager concentration.

– Airlines: US went from many carriers to four dominant ones (American, Delta, United, Southwest).

– Telecom: wireless carriers consolidated globally.

Causes debated: economies of scale in tech, network effects, regulatory failures, declining antitrust enforcement, capital allocation favoring incumbents.

Effects also debated: some find rising markups (De Loecker-Eeckhout), reduced labor share, rising prices. Others argue concentration reflects efficiency in winner-take-most markets.

This is one of the most consequential current debates in economics. Policy responses (Lina Khan's FTC, EU Digital Markets Act, antitrust suits against Google and Meta) signal a shift back toward more aggressive enforcement after decades of consolidation.

title: Pricing Strategy
description: Price discrimination, two-part tariffs, bundling, peak-load pricing

concepts.title: Why Firms Don't Just Set One Price
concepts.contentHtml:
The textbook monopolist sets one price and one quantity. Real firms charge different prices to different customers, in different contexts, at different times.

Why? Because customers value goods differently, and capturing more of the willingness-to-pay raises profits.

If everyone valued a good at $10, charging $10 would extract all surplus. Different customers value it at $5, $8, $15, $30. A single price either turns away the low-value buyers ($30 misses anyone valuing below $30) or leaves money on the table from high-value ones ($10 captures only $10 from a buyer worth $30).

Price discrimination tries to charge different customers different prices reflecting their willingness to pay.

concepts.title: Three Degrees of Price Discrimination
concepts.contentHtml:
Pigou's classification (1920).

First-degree (perfect): charge each customer their exact willingness to pay. Captures all surplus. Rare in practice — would require knowing everyone's reservation price. Approximated by personalized online pricing.

Second-degree: different prices for different quantities or qualities. Customers self-select based on willingness to pay. Examples: bulk discounts, airline classes (economy/business/first), software tiers (basic/pro/enterprise), restaurant menus.

Third-degree: different prices for different identifiable groups. Senior discounts, student tickets, regional pricing, gender-based pricing (controversial).

All three are common; second and third dominate. First-degree is becoming more feasible in digital settings where firms can observe individual behavior.

concepts.title: Two-Part Tariffs
concepts.contentHtml:
A common pricing structure: charge a fixed entry fee plus a per-unit price.

Examples: Costco membership + per-item prices. Phone plans (monthly fee + per-minute charges). Amusement parks (admission + ride tickets, historically). Razors-and-blades. SaaS (subscription + usage).

The economics: with a uniform marginal price equal to marginal cost, the per-unit transactions are efficient (no DWL). The fixed fee captures consumer surplus.

Optimal under known demand: set marginal price = MC, and fixed fee = consumer surplus at that price. Captures all surplus while preserving efficiency.

Tricky when demand varies across consumers. The fixed fee can't be too high (excludes low-demand customers) or too low (leaves surplus on the table from high-demand ones). Costco's model — only allow members, but make the membership low enough to cast wide — is one solution.

concepts.title: Bundling
concepts.contentHtml:
Bundling — selling multiple goods together at a single price — can boost firm profits even when individual goods could be sold separately.

Why? Bundling reduces the variation in customer valuations. If some customers value good A more and some value B more, but the average valuation of (A+B) is more uniform, bundling captures more surplus.

Cable TV is the classic case: 200 channels for one price. Some customers value sports, some news, some entertainment. The bundle captures revenue from all of them.

Microsoft Office bundles Word, Excel, PowerPoint. Amazon Prime bundles shipping, video, music, others. Streaming bundles (Disney+, Netflix tiers).

Bundling is anticompetitive when used by dominant firms to extend market power into adjacent markets — the Microsoft IE/Windows case in the 1990s, current concerns about Apple bundling. Where it leverages dominance, antitrust enforcement gets involved.

concepts.title: Peak-Load and Dynamic Pricing
concepts.contentHtml:
Many goods have demand that varies dramatically over time but capacity that doesn't. Solution: peak-load pricing.

Examples: electricity (spot prices vs flat rates), Uber (surge pricing), airline tickets (more expensive during holidays), hotel rates, theme park admission.

The economics: peak demand causes congestion or capacity shortages. Pricing higher in peak periods both rations demand efficiently and signals when more capacity is valuable.

Time-varying prices can be politically controversial — Uber surge pricing during emergencies generates outrage. The economic answer: surge pricing brings out drivers who'd otherwise stay home; the alternative is shortage. Empirical studies (Hall-Kendrick-Nosko) confirm surge pricing improves welfare on average.

Modern dynamic pricing has expanded with data and computational capacity. Algorithmic pricing in retail, hospitality, and entertainment is now standard. The line between sophisticated price discrimination and exploitation isn't always clear, raising new policy questions.

title: Antitrust & Competition Policy
description: Mergers, predatory pricing, Sherman Act, the consumer welfare standard

concepts.title: Why Antitrust Exists
concepts.contentHtml:
Markets sometimes fail to be competitive. Without intervention, firms can collude to fix prices, monopolists can entrench their positions, and successful firms can buy or destroy competitors.

Antitrust law (or competition law in non-US usage) prohibits these behaviors. The US Sherman Act of 1890 banned 'every contract, combination, or conspiracy in restraint of trade' and 'monopolization' — the original constitutional documents of antitrust.

The economic logic: monopoly produces deadweight loss, distorts innovation, and reduces consumer welfare. Even when individual firms aren't monopolists, anti-competitive agreements among them produce similar harms.

The policy response: detect anticompetitive conduct and structure, prohibit it, sometimes break up offending firms.

concepts.title: Per Se vs Rule of Reason
concepts.contentHtml:
Antitrust violations are evaluated under two standards.

Per se illegal: certain conduct is presumed harmful regardless of effects. Price-fixing among competitors, market allocation, bid-rigging — automatic violations.

Why per se? Because these behaviors are so reliably harmful that case-by-case evaluation costs more than it saves.

Rule of reason: case-by-case analysis of effects. Was the conduct anticompetitive in this specific market? Did it produce efficiencies that offset harms?

Most modern antitrust uses rule of reason. The shift began in the 1970s and accelerated as economic analysis became central to enforcement.

The tradeoff: per se rules are predictable and cheap to enforce. Rule of reason permits beneficial conduct that resembles harmful conduct in form. Most countries have similar bifurcations, though the specific rules vary.

concepts.title: Merger Review
concepts.contentHtml:
Many antitrust matters are mergers: when one firm proposes to buy another, regulators evaluate the competitive effects.

The framework: define the market; assess concentration changes (HHI shifts); analyze entry barriers and likely competitive responses; evaluate efficiency claims.

Pro-competitive mergers (combining complementary capabilities, achieving scale economies) are mostly approved. Anti-competitive mergers (eliminating direct competitors in concentrated markets) are challenged or blocked.

Prominent challenges: AT&T's attempted acquisition of T-Mobile (blocked 2011); Sysco-US Foods (blocked 2015); Microsoft-Activision (approved with conditions 2023). Big tech acquisitions of nascent rivals (Facebook-WhatsApp, Facebook-Instagram, Google-DoubleClick) have come under retroactive review.

The 1980s-2010s saw lenient merger review under the Chicago school's faith in market self-correction. The 2020s have shifted toward more aggressive enforcement, especially for digital platforms.

concepts.title: The Consumer Welfare Standard
concepts.contentHtml:
From the 1970s, US antitrust law was guided by the consumer welfare standard: conduct is anticompetitive when it harms consumers, typically through higher prices.

Robert Bork's The Antitrust Paradox (1978) argued antitrust had drifted from this clear standard toward populist concerns about firm size, fairness, and political power. Bork's framework dominated for forty years.

Critics in recent decades (Tim Wu, Lina Khan, Marshall Steinbaum) argue consumer welfare misses important harms:

– Lower wages from labor monopsony

– Reduced innovation from concentrated markets

– Privacy harms in digital platforms

– Political and democratic concerns about corporate power

– Quality degradation (not just price increases)

The 'New Brandeis' or 'hipster antitrust' movement urges broader scope. Khan's 2017 Yale Law article on Amazon's competitive practices became a movement document; her appointment to FTC chair in 2021 signaled a partial policy shift.

The debate is unresolved. Which standard prevails will shape antitrust enforcement for decades.

concepts.title: International Variation
concepts.contentHtml:
Antitrust enforcement varies considerably across countries.

EU competition law is generally more aggressive than US since the 2000s — bringing major cases against Microsoft, Google, Apple. The EU has been the lead regulator for big tech in many ways.

UK created an independent Competition and Markets Authority in 2014 and has been increasingly active.

China has its own antitrust framework — sometimes used for genuine competition concerns, sometimes as a tool of industrial policy.

Latin America has varying enforcement — Mexico's COFECE has been notably independent; Brazil's CADE has reviewed major mergers.

Developing economies often have antitrust statutes but limited enforcement capacity.

For multinational firms, the highest-bar jurisdiction effectively sets global rules. EU rejection of a merger or finding of monopoly behavior often forces firms to alter conduct globally. This 'Brussels effect' makes EU competition policy a global force despite the EU's smaller market share.

title: Auctions & Bidding
description: English, Dutch, sealed-bid, second-price — strategic bidding and the winner's curse

concepts.title: Four Auction Formats
concepts.contentHtml:
The four canonical auctions:

English (open ascending): auctioneer raises price; bidders drop out; last bidder wins at exit price of last drop-out. Used for art, real estate, eBay.

Dutch (open descending): auctioneer starts high and lowers price; first bidder to accept wins. Used for tulip bulbs, fish in some markets.

First-price sealed bid: all bidders submit secret bids; highest wins, pays their bid. Used for government procurement, some asset sales.

Second-price sealed bid (Vickrey): highest bid wins, but pays the second-highest bid. Used for some online ad auctions.

These look different but have surprising connections.

concepts.title: Strategic Equivalence
concepts.contentHtml:
Some auctions are strategically equivalent.

English ≈ Second-price. In an English auction with private values, you should bid up to your true value (and stop). The price you pay is the second-highest valuation. Same outcome as a second-price sealed bid.

Dutch ≈ First-price. In a Dutch auction, you decide a price at which to accept; this is strategically identical to submitting that price as a sealed bid.

So we really have two basic types: ascending/second-price (where you bid your true value) and descending/first-price (where you bid less than your true value to avoid overpaying).

concepts.title: Truthful Bidding in Second-Price
concepts.contentHtml:
The remarkable property of second-price auctions: bidding your true value is a dominant strategy.

Why? Suppose your true value is $100.

Bid $100. If second-highest is $90, you win and pay $90 (profit $10). If second-highest is $110, you lose (profit $0).

Bid $80 (under-bid). If second-highest is $90, you lose — even though winning at $90 would have profited $10. Worse off.

Bid $120 (over-bid). If second-highest is $110, you win and pay $110 — losing $10. Worse off.

Truth-telling weakly dominates. This is one of the few mechanisms with a clean truth-telling guarantee — a key reason second-price auctions appear in many real settings (Google's ad auction, classic spectrum auctions).

concepts.title: Revenue Equivalence
concepts.contentHtml:
Revenue Equivalence Theorem (Vickrey, 1961; Myerson, 1981): under standard assumptions (private values, risk-neutrality, symmetric bidders, common distribution), all four standard auction formats produce the same expected revenue.

Surprising! It seems like first-price would generate more (bidders bid more to ensure winning) or less (bidders shade bids down). The math says it averages out.

Conditions for equivalence:

– Private (independent) values.

– Risk-neutral bidders.

– Symmetric distribution.

– Highest-value bidder wins.

When conditions fail, equivalence breaks. With risk-averse bidders, first-price raises more revenue (bidders pay extra to reduce the chance of losing). With correlated values (common-value or affiliated values), English auctions raise more (bidders learn from others' drop-outs). With asymmetric bidders, first-price may favor weaker bidders.

The takeaway for auction design: format matters when conditions deviate from the symmetric private-value benchmark — which is most real auctions.

concepts.title: The Winner's Curse
concepts.contentHtml:
In common-value auctions (where the item has the same true value to all bidders, but each estimates it imperfectly), naive bidding leads to the winner's curse.

Setting: oil leases. The oil's value is the same to any winner. Each bidder estimates it; estimates have noise.

The winner is the bidder with the highest estimate — typically biased upward. Winning is bad news: it means you over-estimated.

Sophisticated bidders shade their bids down to account for this. The optimal shade depends on the number of bidders (more bidders → larger expected over-estimation by the winner → more shading).

Real auctions for oil leases, spectrum, and acquisitions show winner's curse effects empirically. Inexperienced bidders systematically over-pay; experienced bidders learn to shade.

The corporate version: winner's curse in M&A. Acquirers who 'win' bidding contests for target companies tend to overpay, generating poor returns. This is one explanation for the empirical underperformance of acquired-firm shareholders.

title: Network Effects & Platforms
description: Two-sided markets, tipping, switching costs, the economics of Big Tech

concepts.title: Network Effects
concepts.contentHtml:
A network effect exists when a product becomes more valuable as more people use it. Phones, languages, social networks, payment systems.

Direct network effects: more users means each user can connect to more others. Telephones, fax machines, social media.

Indirect network effects: more users on one side attract more participants on the other. Credit cards (more cardholders attract more merchants attract more cardholders).

Markets with strong network effects tend toward concentration — sometimes 'tipping' to a single dominant player. The reason: each new user prefers to join the largest network, accelerating its growth.

Classic examples: Microsoft Windows in PCs (1990s), Facebook in social networking, Google in search, WhatsApp in many country markets, Visa/MasterCard in cards.

concepts.title: Tipping and Path Dependence
concepts.contentHtml:
In tipping markets, early advantages can become permanent dominance.

The QWERTY keyboard layout was designed in the 1870s for mechanical typewriters. The Dvorak layout is arguably more efficient. But QWERTY's installed base — millions of trained typists — locked it in. We still use it 150 years later.

VHS beat Betamax despite reportedly inferior quality, because of porn-industry adoption and Hollywood deals.

Facebook beat MySpace partly through real-name policies and college rollout that built denser networks earlier.

The Brian Arthur literature on increasing returns describes this path dependence: early small advantages compound into lasting market structure.

Implications: which platform dominates may not be socially optimal. The market 'picks' a winner via tipping, but the winner isn't necessarily the best alternative — just the one with early momentum.

concepts.title: Two-Sided Markets
concepts.contentHtml:
Two-sided markets have two distinct user groups whose presence each makes the other side more valuable.

Examples: credit cards (cardholders, merchants), operating systems (users, developers), shopping malls (shoppers, retailers), advertising (audience, advertisers), gaming consoles (gamers, game developers), Uber (riders, drivers).

Pricing strategy: subsidize one side to attract the other. Newspapers historically priced low for readers (who attract advertisers). Adobe gives away PDF readers (free) but charges for Acrobat (full version). Search engines are free for users but charge advertisers.

The Rochet-Tirole framework (Nobel 2014) showed that 'who pays' depends on demand elasticities, network strength, and platform competition. The standard intuition (price equals marginal cost) breaks down — it can be optimal to price below marginal cost on one side and above on the other.

concepts.title: Switching Costs and Lock-In
concepts.contentHtml:
Switching costs are what users pay (in money, time, hassle) to change platforms. They're a key determinant of platform power.

Examples:

– Data: all your photos are on iCloud; switching means migration.

– Skills: you've learned Photoshop; learning Affinity Designer takes effort.

– Relationships: all your friends are on Facebook.

– Tooling: your enterprise built workflows on Salesforce; switching to HubSpot means re-architecting.

– Contracts: long-term commitments lock you in.

– Compatibility: non-interoperable ecosystems force all-in commitments.

High switching costs let dominant platforms extract higher prices and reduce service quality without losing users. Even if a competitor offers a better product, the cost of switching may exceed the benefit.

Policy responses include data portability (require platforms to let users export their data — GDPR includes this), interoperability mandates, and open standards. Effectiveness varies; well-implemented portability has been hard to enforce.

concepts.title: Big Tech and Antitrust
concepts.contentHtml:
The major US tech firms — Apple, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft — have dominated their markets for over a decade. Their persistence raises antitrust questions.

The competition concerns:

Self-preferencing: Amazon ranks its own products above competitors; Google's search results favor its services; Apple's App Store rules favor Apple's apps.

Killer acquisitions: Meta acquired Instagram and WhatsApp partly to neutralize potential competitors; Google has acquired hundreds of startups.

Vertical integration: Amazon competes with sellers on its own platform; Apple's hardware-OS-services bundle creates integrated lock-in.

Data advantages: incumbents accumulate user data that competitors can't match.

Major actions:

– EU: $9B+ in fines against Google; Digital Markets Act (2022) imposes structural obligations on 'gatekeepers.'

– US: DOJ won the Google search antitrust case (2024); FTC sued Meta to undo its Instagram/WhatsApp acquisitions; Amazon, Apple cases pending.

– China: 2020-22 crackdown on Alibaba, Tencent, others — partly antitrust, partly political.

The 2020s are likely the most active antitrust period since the early 1900s. Outcomes will shape platform competition for decades.
